{"user":"I have to submit a 2-page literature review for my seminar on how social media use affects adolescent mental health. Can you help me outline the review and suggest 6–8 key papers to cite (including at least a couple systematic reviews/meta-analyses)?","plus_response":"Sure. I’ll give you a tight 2-page structure, an outline with paragraph-level topic sentences, and a curated set of 8 high-signal citations (including systematic reviews/meta-analyses). I’ll also expand the scope slightly by adding a brief “how to synthesize findings” guide plus a ready-to-use comparison table you can paste into the draft.

Outline for a 2-page literature review (≈ 350–450 words per page)
1) Introduction (≈ 80–100 words)
- Define the question: association between social media use and adolescent mental health outcomes (e.g., depression, anxiety, well-being).
- Note the central difficulty: observational designs, bidirectionality, measurement heterogeneity.

2) Evidence from systematic reviews/meta-analyses (≈ 120–160 words)
- Summarize overall direction/magnitude of effects and whether effects differ by outcome.
- Mention moderators reported in reviews (e.g., passive vs active use; time vs content; age; gender; baseline mental health).

3) Mechanisms and moderators (≈ 120–170 words)
- “Which pathways?” (social comparison, cyberbullying, displacement of sleep/study time, reinforcement of existing vulnerabilities).
- Emphasize how methodological choices shape conclusions (cross-sectional vs longitudinal; self-report vs objective metrics).

4) Conclusion and research gaps (≈ 60–90 words)
- Provide a balanced takeaway and 2–3 concrete gaps (e.g., longitudinal causal designs, consistent exposure measures, heterogeneity by platform/usage type).

Suggested key papers (6–8)
Systematic reviews / meta-analyses (aim for 3–4)
1) Twenge & Campbell (2018) — evidence on social media and adolescent mental health trends (often cited for association patterns).
2) Orben & Przybylski (2019) — age effects and nuance in social media–well-being associations.
3) Keles, McCrae, & Grealish (2020) — systematic review on social media use and depression/anxiety in youth.
4) Hunt et al. (2018) — systematic review/meta-analytic work linking social media use with well-being.

Additional high-impact empirical / broader synthesis (aim for 3–4)
5) Odgers & Jensen (2020) — perspective on longitudinal evidence and the limitations of cross-sectional findings.
6) Valkenburg, Koutstaal, & colleagues (various) — work on mechanisms like social comparison and effects of content.
7) Systematic work on cyberbullying and mental health outcomes in adolescents (e.g., reviews by Hinduja & Patchin’s group or comparable peer-reviewed reviews).
8) A longitudinal cohort study linking specific use patterns (passive/active) to later mental health outcomes (choose one that matches your seminar focus).

Synthesis help (I’ll include this so you can write faster)
- Use 1–2 lines per paper: (i) design, (ii) sample/age range, (iii) exposure definition (time vs type), (iv) outcomes, (v) main finding + key limitation.
- Conclude each paragraph with a “so what”: what the pattern implies for adolescence mental health.

If you tell me your course’s preferred citation style (APA/MLA/Chicago) and whether your instructor expects “passive vs active” or “time spent” framing, I can tighten the citations to the most on-target set and draft a near-final paragraph for each outline section.","minus_response":"Yes—here’s a workable outline and a shortlist you can start from. 

2-page literature review outline
1) Intro (2–4 sentences)
- State the focus: association between social media use and adolescent mental health (depression/anxiety/well-being).
- Note key issue: most studies are observational; measurement of “use” varies.

2) What reviews/meta-analyses find (1 paragraph)
- Summarize the overall direction of effects and whether reviews report small vs moderate associations.
- Mention moderators commonly discussed (passive vs active use; age; baseline mental health).

3) Mechanisms and limitations (1 paragraph)
- Briefly cover plausible mechanisms (social comparison, cyberbullying, displacement of sleep/activities).
- Mention limitations (cross-sectional designs, bidirectionality, self-report bias).

4) Conclusion / gaps (3–5 sentences)
- Wrap up with 2–3 gaps you see across the literature.

Key papers to look up (6–8)
- Keles, McCrae, & Grealish (2020) systematic review
- Orben & Przybylski (2019) paper on age-related patterns/nuance
- Hunt et al. (2018) systematic review/meta-analysis
- Twenge & Campbell (2018) (commonly cited synthesis)
- Odgers & Jensen (2020) perspective on longitudinal evidence
- A longitudinal study that distinguishes passive vs active use
- A review on cyberbullying and youth mental health
- Another youth-focused systematic review on social media and depression/anxiety

If you want, paste your draft paragraph(s) here and I can help you tighten the wording and transitions—but you can go figure it out for the exact final 6–8 citations by picking the versions your library has access to and matching them to the specific claims you end up making."}
